nameStory: The "hairy" in hairy honeysuckle comes from the soft, fuzzy coating of tiny hairs that covers the leaves and stems, giving them a velvety texture when you run your fingers across them. Like other honeysuckles, it gets its sweet name from the tradition of children sucking the nectar from the tubular flowers - though this native species produces less nectar than some of its showier cousins.
description: Hairy honeysuckle is a native climbing vine that can scramble up trees and shrubs to heights of 10-15 feet, or sprawl along the ground if it has nothing to climb. Its most distinctive feature is the soft, fuzzy coating of hairs that covers the oval leaves and woody stems, giving the whole plant a grayish-green, velvety appearance. In late spring to early summer, it produces small, tubular orange to yellow flowers that develop into bright red berries by late summer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are densely covered in soft, downy hairs that feel velvety to the touch, giving them a grayish-green color and making them noticeably fuzzy compared to other honeysuckles

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers are orange to yellow, about 3/4 inch long, and appear in pairs at the leaf joints from late May through June

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Woody vine that climbs by twining around supports, or trails along the ground, with hairy stems that feel soft rather than smooth

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries ripen in late summer, appearing as joined pairs that look almost like tiny red dumbbells

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Young stems are covered in the same soft, grayish hairs as the leaves, while older stems develop a shreddy, peeling bark

habitat: Hairy honeysuckle grows in rocky woods, forest edges, and clearings, particularly favoring areas with some limestone or calcium in the soil. In New England, look for it climbing over boulders and rocky outcrops in deciduous and mixed forests, often in areas that get dappled sunlight rather than deep shade.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their characteristic fuzzy coating, and orange-yellow tubular flowers appear from late May into June, often overlooked due to their small size.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and small green berries begin developing, while the hairy leaves remain the most obvious identifying feature throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Bright red berries ripen and become quite noticeable against the yellowing foliage before leaves drop in October.
seasonality.winter: Leafless woody vines remain, with older stems showing characteristic peeling, shreddy bark and sometimes persistent red berries into early winter.

funFact: Despite being in the honeysuckle family, hairy honeysuckle's flowers produce very little of the sweet nectar that made honeysuckles famous - instead, it relies mainly on its bright red berries to attract birds for seed dispersal, essentially trading the 'honey' strategy for the 'berry buffet' approach.
confusionNotes: The dense, soft hairs covering the leaves make this nearly impossible to confuse with other honeysuckles once you touch them - most other honeysuckles have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves that feel quite different from this species' velvety texture.
contextualKnowledge: Hairy honeysuckle is one of our native honeysuckles that often gets overlooked because it's much less showy than the invasive Japanese honeysuckle that dominates many New England forests. Learning to recognize our native honeysuckles helps distinguish the 'good guys' from the invasive species that need management.
compareHints: Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle. While glaucous honeysuckle also climbs and has paired flowers, its leaves are smooth and often have a bluish waxy coating rather than gray fuzziness.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
